findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime-ordered querysets, breaking the audit log endpoint path that uses it
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw model attribute, which only works for numeric keys. The new code in organization_auditlogs.py instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a datetime and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError (this is exactly why DateTimePaginator overrides get_item_key to convert via strftime). Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value, which build_queryset then compares against a datetime column. Every request with `optimized_pagination=true` will therefore 500 on the first page when build_cursor calls the key function. The optimized branch added to OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint is non-functional as written.

findings.title: Negative-offset 'advanced pagination' path crashes: Django does not support negative slicing
findings.body: The new branch `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` passes a negative start directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and the comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django's QuerySet slicing raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative start. Cursor offsets are user-controllable (Cursor.from_string happily parses `value:-100:0`), so any caller that enables this flag — the audit log endpoint does so via `enable_advanced_features=True` — can be forced into an unhandled exception and a 500 on every such request. The misleading comment in Cursor.__init__ (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py) about negative offsets being a supported optimization compounds this.

findings.title: organization_context.member can be None, causing AttributeError for non-member authentication
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally whenever the user is not a superuser. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional — requests authenticated with org-level auth tokens or other non-member principals have no member object — so those requests to the audit log endpoint will now raise AttributeError and return 500 instead of the audit log. This access is new in this PR; previously the endpoint never touched `.member`. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

findings.title: Segment keys change Redis type from SET to ZSET with no key rename or migration, causing WRONGTYPE errors during rollout
findings.body: This PR changes the segment storage under the same key pattern `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` from a Redis SET (sadd/sscan/sunionstore) to a ZSET (zadd/zscan/zunionstore). Keys written by the old code live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s). After deploy, the Python `p.zadd(...)` and the new Lua script's `zcard`/`zunionstore` will hit pre-existing SET keys and Redis will raise WRONGTYPE, which propagates out of process_spans and fails the whole consumer batch (crash/retry loop) until all old keys expire. The key namespace should be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:sz:`) or a migration/compat path provided.

findings.title: KeyError on spans missing end_timestamp_precise will fail the entire batch
findings.body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing on the decoded span payload. Any message from an older Relay or a producer that omits this field raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and leaves the consumer stuck retrying the same poison message. The pre-existing test payload (which lacked the field and had to be updated in this PR) shows such messages exist in practice. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` with a sensible fallback (e.g. 0 or the batch timestamp) so one malformed span cannot stall processing.

findings.title: Segment span cap is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (1001) is now dead config
findings.body: The eviction logic `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` hardcodes the limit in the Lua script instead of taking it as an ARGV, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` — a parameter that is no longer read anywhere after this PR removed the `max_segment_spans` check (and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) from `_load_segment_data`. Operators tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect, and the two values (1000 vs 1001) already disagree. Either pass the limit into the script or remove the Python config.

findings.title: Redirect-chain resolution limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
findings.body: The redirect-following loop was reduced from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment warning that segment trees deeper than the limit 'may not be joined together correctly' was deleted rather than updated. Segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now silently fail to merge and be flushed as split/duplicated segments — a 10x tightening of a correctness-relevant limit with no mention in the PR and no remaining in-code warning. If intentional for performance, the comment should be kept (updated to 1000) and the behavior change documented; the redirect_depth metrics already emitted can verify impact.

findings.title: Comment claims negative offsets are 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' — queryset actually raises
findings.body: The new comment above `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` says allowing negative offsets 'is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. In fact Django raises AssertionError on negative slice starts, which is precisely why the clamp to max(0, offset) had to be added. The comment describes the opposite of what the code does and contradicts the identical false claim in OptimizedCursorPaginator; it should be corrected so future readers don't remove the clamp believing the ORM handles it.
